title: When the world changes
teaches: Change detection: observations against a reference map, independent evidence, triage by risk, human review tiers, and safe publishing and rollback

parts.title: A slur on the map of New York

blocks.text: On 30 August 2018, people using Snapchat, the Citi Bike app, the property site StreetEasy and other apps saw New York City labelled on their maps with an antisemitic slur. All of the apps drew their maps from Mapbox, a company that supplies map data and map rendering to thousands of applications, and Mapbox's data draws on several sources, including OpenStreetMap, which anyone can edit. The label was live for about four hours, and Mapbox removed it within an hour of a customer reporting it. The same day its chief executive, Eric Gundersen, said the name had been changed by a vandal. Mapbox said the edit came in through one of its data sources; it did not say which, and Gundersen cautioned against blaming OpenStreetMap's volunteers.[^mapbox]

Mapbox's own account explained how the edit got through. Its review tool had marked the edit as significant, because it changed a major feature, and sent it to a person. That person was one of the reviewers who together worked through more than 70,000 flagged changes a day, and approved it, and the decision reached every map that showed New York. Mapbox's changes afterwards included redundant review, so that one person could not be a single point of failure, and weighting each change by how much it would affect customers.

In this lesson, we will design the system that keeps the fleet's world map from lesson P3 in step with a changing world. Roads close, turns are banned, shops move, and the fleet's cameras, users' reports and outside sources all notice. The system must find the changes, decide which ones to believe, publish them quickly, and stop a wrong label on a prominent place from reaching every user.

parts.title: What it must do, and what it need not

blocks.text: **Functional.** The system must collect observations that disagree with the current map; group observations of the same change; compute a confidence score indicating whether each change is real; decide by risk tier whether an edit is published automatically, reviewed by one person, or reviewed by two independent reviewers; publish accepted changes through the validation checks of lesson P4; and roll back any single change or all changes from a specified source quickly.

**Non-functional.** A road closure should reach the map within hours; a moved shop within days is fine. The more people a change reaches, the rarer a wrong one must be. Reviewers' time is the scarce resource, so it must go to the changes where a person's judgement matters most.
**Out of scope.** We will not design the detectors that read signs and lane markings from camera images, or the labelling platform the reviewers' tools are built on (lesson P2).

A **change** starts as an **observation** that disagrees with the map: a camera on a fleet vehicle reads a no-left-turn sign at a junction where the map allows the turn, phones stop driving down a road that the map says is open (the traffic data of lesson M4), a user reports that a shop has closed, a city publishes a list of road works. One observation proves little. Detectors misread signs, phones take detours for many reasons, and some reports are mistakes or vandalism.

Confidence comes from **independent** observations that agree. Two cameras on different vehicles on different days reading the same sign count for much more than two readings from one vehicle a second apart, which share the same lighting, the same lens and the same misreading. Ten reports from one account count once. Observations that share a source, such as a vehicle, an account or a device, are grouped and counted as one, the same group leakage that lesson P1 guarded against when splitting evaluation data, and the spoofed phones of lesson M4, which sent fake positions to fake a traffic jam, are the reason to check. Within one source, more observations in a short time add almost nothing: ten readings from one vehicle in a minute are one. Across independent sources, agreement at the same time is strong evidence, as when a real closure makes many vehicles detour at once. Cameras that run the same detector model also share its systematic misreadings, so agreement among vehicles on one software version counts for less than the number of vehicles suggests. An account's record counts too: a report from an account whose past reports were usually right starts with more confidence than one from an account created yesterday. The system combines the independent evidence for each proposed change into a confidence score, and lesson P2's calibration rule applies: among changes scored at 95%, about 95% should turn out to be real, checked on a sample that people verify.

Confidence is one axis; the other is the cost of an error. The impact of an erroneous change scales with the size of the audience exposed to it and the severity of the disruption. A relocated shop entrance affects a few hundred visitors and costs each of them a short walk. An incorrect turn restriction alters routing for thousands of drivers. A falsely closed motorway or an altered city name affects millions of users. The system assigns each proposed change a **risk tier** determined by the feature type and the **prominence** of the location, quantified by historical query volume and routing throughput. Feature types have baseline tiers: a shop is low, a road rule is medium, and a closure or place name is high. A change affecting an exceptionally prominent location is promoted by one risk tier, so altering a business name in Times Square receives the same scrutiny as a new turn restriction.

Each tier follows a distinct review path. Low-risk changes with confidence scores above the operational threshold are published automatically. All other proposals require human review. The medium tier requires one reviewer. The highest tier (national and municipal names, major motorway closures, and edits to the most heavily viewed map tiles) requires **two reviewers** who evaluate the change independently, ensuring that an oversight by a single operator cannot reach millions of screens. Reviewers draw tasks from a queue using the task leases and qualification checks introduced in lesson P2. An individual reviewer processes roughly 400 changes a day; reviewing 10,000 proposed changes a day without automated publishing would require 25 full-time reviewers. Because human review capacity is constrained on any given day, adjusting the confidence threshold for automated publishing directly controls the volume of work diverted to the queue.

blocks.caption: A day of proposed map changes. The threshold decides how many low-risk changes skip people; the reviewers' capacity decides whether a queue builds. Rates are round figures of our own.
blocks.task: Assign two reviewers to the high-risk tier, keep the wait under 24 hours, and keep erroneous data under 100,000 views a day

blocks.text: The queue behaves like the server of lesson 2. Reviewers take the highest-risk and most urgent changes first, so when reviews arrive faster than reviewers can do them, the overload shows first as low-risk changes waiting longer and longer, and then, once the priority work alone exceeds capacity, as closures slipping too. A new change waits about the queue length divided by the rate of review: 2,000 changes waiting for reviewers who clear 4,000 a day is half a day. In a stable queue, Little's law (queue length equals arrival rate times average wait) gives the same relation between the averages. A higher bar for automatic publishing makes each automatic change safer and sends more work to people, so beyond some point it makes the system worse: once more changes reach people each day than they can clear, the queue grows every day and every change waits longer. In a model with the figure's rates, most of the wrong data that reaches users comes from the middle tier. The low tier reaches few people and the high tier gets two reviewers, while the middle tier has neither protection and is common enough to add up.

Accepted changes do not go straight into the map. They are applied to the next version through the pipeline of lesson P3 and pass through the checks of lesson P4 before the pointer moves, so a change that would, for example, disconnect a motorway from the rest of the road graph (the roads as links between junctions) is caught even after a person approved it. Urgent changes, such as a closure for a fire reported by the fire service or confirmed by many vehicles, can be published after one reviewer's approval to the routing service's live overlay, a small layer of temporary changes applied on top of the published map, within minutes, and folded into the next full version later. An urgent closure that no further evidence confirms expires from the overlay after a set time, so a false report cannot close a road indefinitely.

Every change carries its evidence and its source, so it can be **rolled back** on its own, and so can every change from one source or one account at once. When a vandal is found, the system lists every change that account's observations contributed to and reverts them as a batch. Some of those features may have been edited again since, by other people with good evidence, so the batch goes through review and the checks of lesson P4 like any other change rather than being applied blindly. A rollback is itself a change, published as a new version, so the history of the map stays intact.

The system also watches its own outcome. Users' error reports, routes that people stop following, and later fleet observations that contradict a published change are all evidence that a change was wrong. Each wrong change that got through is traced back to the tier and the decision that let it through, and the thresholds are adjusted, the way an error budget is managed in lesson 24: each wrong change uses some of a tier's allowance, and a tier that overspends gets a stricter threshold.

OpenStreetMap relies on its community to review edits after they are made. Volunteers watch changes in their areas with tools such as OSMCha, which flags suspicious edits; it was started by Wille Marcel in 2015, long supported by Mapbox, and has been a project of OpenStreetMap US since 2023. Data consumers such as Mapbox add their own filtering before they publish, and Google Maps reviews the edits its users suggest before they appear.

Mapbox's account of the New York incident describes the same parts as this lesson: a tool that scores changes and sends the significant ones to people, and, after the incident, a second, redundant review and a weight for each change's effect on customers.

parts.title: At ten and a hundred times

blocks.text: **At ten times** (100,000 proposed changes a day), review teams are partitioned by geographic region and language fluency. The work queue is sharded regionally, with review staffing provisioned to match local arrival rates. Automated publishing processes the majority of low-risk proposals, and a fixed random sample of automated approvals is audited daily to measure the empirical error rate.

**At a hundred times**, the observations come mostly from fleets and phones rather than people, and change detection becomes a streaming system: observations are matched to map features as they arrive, grouped by feature and evidence source in windows, and scored continuously, with the techniques of lesson 17. People review only the highest tiers and samples of everything else, and the measurements of how often each tier is wrong become the system's main control.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on keeping a map in step with the world
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A proposed change renames a capital city. The automated checks flag it as significant, because it touches a major feature, and one reviewer approves it. Which design change most directly prevents a repeat?
choices: Lowering the confidence threshold for automatic publishing in every tier
A second automated check that compares new names with a list of known offensive terms
Requiring two independent reviewers for changes to the most prominent names and roads
items.why: The automation worked and one person's decision failed. For changes that reach millions of people, two independent reviewers make a single slip harmless.

items.ask: Ten observations of a new turn ban arrive within one minute, all from one vehicle's camera. How should the system count them?
choices: As roughly one piece of evidence, because they share a vehicle, a camera and a moment
As ten pieces of evidence, enough to publish automatically
As ten pieces of evidence, but published only after a person checks one
items.why: Observations that share a source share its errors. Confidence comes from independent observations that agree: different vehicles, days and sources.

items.ask: The team raises the bar for automatic publishing from 80% to 99% confidence, with the same number of reviewers working one queue in arrival order. A week later road closures take days to appear. Why?
choices: The higher bar makes the automated checks slower to run
Fewer low-risk changes publish automatically, so the review queue grows beyond the reviewers' capacity and everything waits behind it
Road closures are always published automatically, and the higher bar now blocks them
items.why: Every change that fails the automatic bar becomes work for the fixed pool of reviewers. When arrivals exceed capacity the queue grows each day, and a new change waits about the queue length divided by the review rate.

items.ask: What should decide a change's risk tier?
choices: What kind of change it is and how many people view or route through that part of the map
The confidence score of the evidence for it
Which source proposed it
items.why: Risk is the cost of being wrong, which grows with how many people a change reaches and how much it affects them. Confidence is a separate axis.

items.ask: A change to a junction's turn rules is placed, correctly, in the middle tier, and one reviewer approves it. Applied to the map, it would cut a motorway off from the rest of the road network. How can the system still catch it?
choices: A second reviewer for every turn-rule change
A rule that turn changes publish only after a week
Approved changes go into the next version and through the publish checks, which test whole-graph invariants such as connectivity
items.why: Review and publish checks catch different things. A person judges whether a change is real; the checks of lesson P4 test whether the resulting map still makes sense as a whole. A second reviewer can miss what the first missed, and waiting a week only delays the damage.

items.ask: An account is found to have submitted many false reports over a month. What makes cleaning up quick?
choices: Rolling the whole map back to the version from a month ago
Every change records the observations and sources behind it, so all changes that relied on the account can be listed and rolled back together
Raising the confidence needed from that kind of report
items.why: Provenance on each change makes rollback by source possible. Rolling back the whole map would also undo a month of real changes, and a higher threshold protects only future changes.

items.ask: In the figure, most of the wrong data reaching users comes from the medium tier. What is the reason?
choices: Medium-tier changes are common enough to add up and prominent enough to matter, but too many to review twice
Medium-tier changes are reviewed by less experienced people
Medium-tier changes publish automatically once confident
items.why: The low tier reaches few people and the high tier gets two reviewers; the middle tier has neither protection, so the system measures it closely and adjusts its thresholds.

summary: **A change needs independent evidence.** One observation that disagrees with the map proves little, since detectors misread and phones detour, and observations that share a source count as one.
**Confidence scores must be calibrated.** Among changes scored at 95%, about 95% should be real, checked on a sample that people verify.

**Review effort follows risk, not confidence alone.** Risk is how many people a wrong change would reach and what it would cost them, so the most prominent names and roads get two independent reviewers.
**Every change stays reversible by source.** Approved changes still pass whole-map checks, and provenance lets every change from one source be reverted at once.

mapbox.title: Where the edit came from
mapbox.text: Mapbox's post, "Zero tolerance for hate speech", published on 30 August 2018, said the edit had come in through one of its data sources, and that its tool had flagged it and a reviewer had approved it. Gundersen told TechCrunch the same day that OpenStreetMap was only one part of what Mapbox used, and cautioned against blaming its volunteer community.
